problem: Navigation agents trained in simulation (even on ProcTHOR-10K) fail to transfer to real homes and offices because of the gap between the training scene distribution and the target environment, and they are brittle to clutter, lighting changes and moved objects. Static reconstructions of the target overfit and are also fragile.
motivation: Real deployment needs agents that are effective in one specific space and also robust to everyday chaos such as moved furniture, people and lighting. The authors observe that a cheap phone scan of layout and large furniture can condition procedural generation, giving many semantically similar but randomized training scenes.
key_idea: Scan the target environment with an iPhone (RoomPlan) to get layout and large-object boxes, then procedurally generate thousands of randomized variants (objects, small items, clutter, materials, lighting) with ProcTHOR and fine-tune an RGB-only ObjectNav policy on them.
insight: Training on a distribution conditioned on the scan gives both specialization and robustness. The privileged model trained on a 5-day hand-built replica matches Phone2Proc on the undisturbed scene but collapses when objects move, clutter is added, people move, or the FOV changes, while Phone2Proc holds up. A logistic regression shows Phone2Proc gives 1.39x odds of success (p<0.0001).
method: Phone scan: an iOS app using Apple RoomPlan outputs a USDZ template with walls, doors and windows, plus 3D boxes for large objects in 16 categories; small objects are ignored.
Conditional layout generation: wall, room, door and window placement is parsed into ProcTHOR, and walls are not restricted to orthogonal axes.
Semantic object sampling: for each scanned object, ProcTHOR assets of a matching type with 3D-box IoU of at least 75% are sampled uniformly, with collision checks (1,633 assets, 108 types).
Randomization: small objects on surfaces, floor clutter, materials, and lights (intensity, RGB, shadows) are randomized, giving about 1000 scene variants per hour on 8 GPUs.

Policy: EmbCLIP-style frozen CLIP-ResNet50 plus GRU, pretrained on ProcTHOR-10K and fine-tuned per environment on 1K variants. Fine-tuning uses lr 3e-5, a -0.05 collision penalty, action noise and randomized FOV.
Real deployment: zero-shot transfer to a LoCoBot with RGB only, discrete actions, 250 or 500 step limits.

setting.training_data: Pretrained on ProcTHOR-10K, then fine-tuned on 1K Phone2Proc procedurally generated variants of each scanned target environment (5M steps for the baseline fine-tune)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB only (no depth, no localization)
setting.action_space: discrete: move ahead 25 cm, rotate left/right 30°, look up/down 30°, done
setting.privileged: none at test time (the Phone2Proc scan is of the target space); the upper-bound baseline OneSim uses a hand-built replica of the scene

numbers.extra: environment-specific fine-tune on 1K scan-conditioned variants; 234 real trials in 5 environments; sim-to-real; step limit 250 or 500
numbers.evidence: In aggregate, Phone2Proc achieves a Success Rate of 70.68% compared to 34.68% for ProcTHOR.

numbers.eval_set_note: 9 episodes (3 objects: bed, sofa, TV) since Habitat covers only those
numbers.evidence: Table 1: Results of 9 trajectories evaluated in RoboTHOR-Real.

numbers_note: Per-environment success rates appear only in a figure (15 trials each) and are not in the text. The 70.68 aggregate is the only text figure; the intro rounds it to 70.7% versus the baseline's 34.7%.
results: Across 234 real-world episodes in 5 environments, Phone2Proc reaches 70.68% SR versus 34.68% for the ProcTHOR baseline. On RoboTHOR-Real it matches the privileged hand-built replica model, and on 9 episodes it beats the Habitat and ProcTHOR baselines (77.8 vs 33.3 SR). It stays robust to clutter, moved objects, people, lighting and FOV changes, where the replica-trained model fails.
limitations: The most common failure is semantic confusion (a covered couch taken for a bed, jugs taken for a vase) because asset diversity is limited (for example only 6 vase models).
Evaluation covers 5 objects and 5 environments with 15 trials each, using environment-specific fine-tuning per scan and a slow real-time rate of about 0.25 FPS.
The scan captures only large objects (16 categories), and novel object categories are not modeled.
